Dr Mattear has been a little better for two days, and seems to steal away, as he
lived, gently and silently — while his wife is bustling up all the stores of furniture
and useful preparations, as necessary for a new and gay establishment. This may be
wise, but not very attractive in a wife who for above forty years I believe was never
thwarted even in her follies by a man every way fitted to take a lead — but nought
of this to Mrs C. I have sent to the Doctor to know the white powder, which I
suppose is Epsom salts. I do not think she will go off with a Major though even an
honest fellow.
I agree with you in what you say of Tom, and also that it may be a loss to him
(for a short time) the separation from his parents, and particularly his brother, but
everything is mixed. Rejoice that he is at present well and happy, perfectly well and
that his mind is of that lovely texture which will ever be attached to those of similar
dispositions, and when home becomes more attractive, by variety and boyish liberty
of which he at present enjoys so much more than he can do in Dublin, it will have
every charm for him. The attention of strangers and even servants here affords him
much pleasure. With you, the latter were quite deficient in attractions for children,
but he will soon be above these, and his brother will take place of every companion,
if he does not come behind him and throw a stone at his head which he really did the
first day he last came to C[abin] Hill], and the impression will not be effaced from
Tom’s mind but by that love which afterwards sweet little William evinced for him.
I shall attend to all you say, for there will be little trouble in keeping the lovely
mind of this captivating boy clear of improper impressions at the age he will be with
me, and I never tried to enforce one, that I did not succeed. Of the effect of this five
year old one, let the voice of others (less partial) judge. They will not pronounce him
a prodigy but everyone announces him the most agreeable child they ever saw, and
that is just up to my highest wish now — practical goodness hereafter completes it.
I am glad the wine pleases you, but that makes me regret that my trip to Dublin
prevented a renewal for next year as it must be a year in the cask. It does well for what
is called house use. I hope the Thwaiteses use at least one bottle a day in that way. I
suppose you got about three dozen and a half. My sister has tried one of your hams,
which is safe and excellent. Long may we thus be of mutual pleasure and comfort.
Dr Bruce sent your letter immediately on his arrival. He called at Dr Mattear’s,
sat half an hour, told him all the news, and that Dr D had recovered his mother.”
Orr has added his mite, by saying he added many years to Miss Dennisor’s life in
the same disorder. I hope William will write soon and mention Mrs Bruce. But as
he will expect something by Orr (and he will never again I think put his letter in a
trunk) I shall now suggest some matter more applicable to himself.
I believe Miss Hutton came down with Dr B but is hard to say when either
